splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on the timing requirements for actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability under ERISA. The resolution affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that plan actuaries may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, as long as the assumptions are applied to data as of that date.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be fixed by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability about potential liability.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: GCIU-Employer Retirement Fund v. Goldfarb Corp.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, pausing the clock and allowing revocation proceedings even after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: No tolling
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is not tolled during absconding because no statutory provision authorizes such tolling, and courts lack inherent authority to extend punishment beyond the judicially imposed term.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1)—which prohibits raising any claim previously presented—in addition to § 2255(h)'s requirements for successive motions. The answer determines whether federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress intended.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring any claim previously presented.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of showing newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits have disagreed on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The resolution affects the ability to challenge rules on mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and election administration practices nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election rules before an election because such rules can affect their competitive position and chances of winning.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not automatically have Article III standing to challenge election rules and must demonstrate a concrete, particularized injury traceable to the challenged law.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether lenity or agency deference prevails when the Sentencing Guidelines or related criminal provisions are ambiguous. At least three circuits hold lenity trumps deference, while the Third Circuit held deference trumps lenity. This split implicates the scope of criminal liability and has been further complicated by the Supreme Court's decision in Loper Bright overruling Chevron.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal statutes or guidelines, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes precedence over the rule of lenity, permitting deference to anti-defendant readings of ambiguous criminal provisions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines commentary (Application Note 1) can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2, which adds inchoate offenses (conspiracy, attempt, aiding and abetting) to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor, or impermissibly expands the guideline text. This affects career-offender sentencing enhancements for many federal defendants.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the career-offender guideline entitled to deference under Stinson, and thus inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, and Application Note 1 impermissibly adds to the guideline rather than interpreting it, making it ineligible for Kisor deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (all three criminal-history criteria must be met to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), or if possessing any single criterion is disqualifying. The split produces dramatically different mandatory minimum sentencing outcomes depending on the circuit, creating severe sentencing disparities.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' means 'and,' so defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1).

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion is disqualifying
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' in this context functions as 'or,' so possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state controls a substance not listed on the federal schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires that the underlying substance be federally scheduled, or whether any state-scheduled substance qualifies. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State-only controlled substances qualify
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include any offense under state law, even if the substance is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

positions.label: Substance must be federally scheduled
positions.summary: Holds that a prior conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines only if the substance is also controlled under federal law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the government needs reasonable suspicion to conduct a forensic search of a cell phone at the border, as opposed to a manual search.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on the level of suspicion required for forensic searches of cell phones at the border. While all circuits agree that manual searches require no individualized suspicion, they disagree on whether the more intrusive forensic searches require reasonable suspicion. This tension arises from competing lines of Supreme Court precedent on border searches and digital privacy.

positions.label: Reasonable suspicion required for forensic searches
positions.summary: Holds that forensic cell phone searches at the border require reasonable suspicion because such searches are qualitatively different and more intrusive than routine border inspections.

positions.label: No reasonable suspicion required for forensic searches
positions.summary: Holds that no individualized suspicion is required for any border search of a cell phone, whether manual or forensic, because border searches are per se reasonable.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Due Process Clause recognizes a 'state-created danger' exception to the general rule that the government has no affirmative duty to protect individuals from privately inflicted harm.
splits.description: Most circuits have recognized a state-created danger doctrine as an exception to the DeShaney no-duty-to-protect rule, but the Fifth Circuit has never adopted it. The circuits that recognize the doctrine disagree on its precise contours and elements, creating inconsistent standards for § 1983 liability when government actors affirmatively create or increase danger to individuals.

positions.label: State-created danger doctrine recognized
positions.summary: Holds that the Due Process Clause permits § 1983 liability when government officials affirmatively create or increase the danger of private violence to an individual, subject to various multi-factor tests.

positions.label: State-created danger doctrine not recognized
positions.summary: Holds that the circuit has never adopted a state-created danger exception and declines to do so, maintaining the general DeShaney rule that government has no duty to protect against private harms.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose punishment for the underlying violation of supervised release conditions at revocation, or whether revocation sanctions must be limited to sanctioning the breach of trust.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether supervised release revocation sentences may punish the defendant for the conduct that violated supervised release conditions or only for the breach of the court's trust. The Sixth Circuit permits punishment for the violation itself, which critics argue contravenes the statutory text and Supreme Court precedent, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split.

positions.label: May punish for the violation conduct
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly impose punishment at revocation for the violations of supervised release conditions, not just the breach of trust.

positions.label: Must sanction only the breach of trust
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of revocation sanctions is to punish the breach of the court's trust inherent in violating supervised release conditions, not to punish the underlying criminal conduct itself.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement (U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6)) permitting such consideration exceeds its statutory authority.
splits.description: Circuits are deeply divided on whether non-retroactive sentencing law changes can support compassionate release, with some holding the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement validly authorizes courts to consider such changes, and others holding it exceeds the Commission's authority. This affects many prisoners serving stacked § 924(c) sentences and other lengthy terms that would be shorter under current law.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, and that the Sentencing Commission exceeded its statutory authority in attempting to provide otherwise.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's policy statement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging the conditions or terms of their confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring civil rights claims, and specifically whether challenges to BOP decisions on First Step Act earned time credits are cognizable in habeas under 28 U.S.C. § 2241.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for prisoners challenging conditions of confinement that affect the duration of custody, or whether civil rights actions are also available. This split has evolved to encompass disputes over BOP implementation of First Step Act time credits and transfer decisions. The Supreme Court has acknowledged but not resolved this question.

positions.label: Habeas is available for BOP custody decisions
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions on earned time credits and transfer to prerelease custody under the First Step Act are cognizable as habeas claims under § 2241 because they affect the duration of confinement.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Woodall v. Federal Bureau of Prisons

positions.label: Habeas is not the proper vehicle
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP administrative decisions regarding conditions of confinement, including transfer and halfway house placement, must be brought under general federal question jurisdiction or the APA rather than habeas.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees filed in a criminal case.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether the 30-day criminal deadline or the 60-day civil deadline for filing a notice of appeal applies to orders resolving Hyde Amendment motions. Because the Hyde Amendment authorizes fees in criminal cases but the motion is considered a civil ancillary proceeding, the characterization determines the applicable filing deadline.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 60-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that because the Hyde Amendment motion arises in a criminal case, the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's property belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor when a Chapter 13 case is converted in good faith to Chapter 7.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 348(f)(1)(A) of the Bankruptcy Code means that appreciation in property value between the Chapter 13 filing and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held appreciation belongs to the estate, which the dissent noted creates a circuit split with courts holding the appreciation belongs to the debtor.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), combined with the broad scope of 'property of the estate' under § 541(a), means post-petition appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure, purpose, and legislative history indicate that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor in a good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents referencing medical treatments and diagnoses is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denials of motions to seal medical information qualify for immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment. Other circuits have not uniformly recognized this category of orders as immediately appealable, creating potential divergence in appellate jurisdiction standards.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable because maintaining medical privacy is a value of 'high order' that would be lost if review is delayed until final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because the privacy interest can be adequately vindicated through other means or on appeal from final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve differing approaches among circuits regarding liability standards for discrimination in hospitality and business establishments. The Court's review of the Second Circuit's approach suggests a circuit split on the applicable legal framework for such claims. SCOTUS resolved this split.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied a particular legal framework for evaluating discrimination claims in hospitality establishments that the Supreme Court found sufficiently important or unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Other circuits' approach
positions.summary: Applied different standards for evaluating discrimination or unfair treatment claims against business establishments, creating the split that prompted SCOTUS review.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
